Custom Templates

Garrett Johnson

October 27, 2026

Overview

It is possible to create your own templates and even extend the abilities of the template system.

The system relies on 3 components:

  • Terms
  • Replacer
  • Templater

Terms

There are several classes that make up the terms section:

  • (DisplayTerm)[#DisplayTerm]
  • (DisplayString)[#DisplayString]
  • (DisplayNone)[#DisplayNone]
  • (DisplayTerms)[#DisplayTerms]
  • (DisplayHeader)[#DisplayHeader]

DisplayTerm

This is the base class that you can extend to create subclasses for custom processing.

These classes need the following methods implemented:

  • active:
    • contents(value): Implement logic to only allow in your desired data types
  • public:
    • makeText: The main method that turns the contents into the replacement string
    • initialize: Initialization of the subclass
      • You only need to add this if you want to pass different defaults
    • addTerms(terms): Implement logic to add more terms to an existing instance

This class has the following parameters:

  • contents: The contents of the class, which will depend on your implementation
  • separators: How many separators should be used when processing the contents
  • trailing_mode: If the processed string should be appended with the separators
  • separator: The separator characters to use when joining or trailing the text

There are also several helper methods:

  • getSeparators(): Gets the separate string to use
    • Typically used to combine the multiple objects in the contents
  • trailing(content): Takes a character and handles applying trailing to it

For example, this is the implementation of DisplayString:

#' DisplayString
#' A class for displaying strings
#' @importFrom checkmate assertCharacter assertVector
#' @export
DisplayString <- R6::R6Class(
  "DisplayString",
  inherit = DisplayTerm,
  active = list(
    #' @field contents A vector of replacement strings
    contents = \(value) {
      if(missing(value)) {
        return(private$.contents)
      }
      if(!is.vector(value)) {
        value <- c(value)
      }
      checkmate::assertVector(value, min.len = 0, names = "unnamed")
      checkmate::assertCharacter(value)
      private$.contents <- value
    }
  ),
  public = list(
    #' @description Initialize a new `DisplayString` object
    #' @param contents The contents of the `DisplayString`
    #' @param separators How many separators to use between the contents
    #' @param trailing_mode If the contents should be trailed by the separtors
    #' @param separator The separating characters (typically `\\n`)
    #' @return A new `DisplayString` object
    initialize = \(contents, separators = 0,
                   trailing_mode = FALSE, separator = "\n") {
      if(missing(contents)) {
        contents <- character()
      }
      super$initialize(contents = contents,
                       separators = separators,
                       trailing_mode = trailing_mode,
                       separator = separator)
    },
    #' @description Generates the string to insert
    #' @returns The display text
    makeText = \() {
      body <- paste(self$contents, collapse = self$getSeparators())
      return(self$trailing(body))
    },
    #' @description Adds a terms terms to the contents
    #' @param terms A character or a vector of character objects
    addTerms = \(terms) {
      #' Adds a terms terms to the contents
      if(!is.vector(terms)) {
        terms <- c(terms)
      }
      checkmate::assertVector(value, min.len = 1, names = "unnamed")
      checkmate::assertCharacter(value)
      self$contents <- c(private$.contents, terms)
      return(invisible(self))
    }
  )
)

DisplayString

DisplayString is the basic class to handle creating text. It simply just takes a character or a vector of characters.

DisplayStrings are created like:

ex_c <- DisplayString$new(
  contents = c("Line 1", "Line 2", "Line 3"),
  separators = "2",
  trailing_mode = FALSE,
  separator = "\n")
ex_text <- ex_c$makeText()

DisplayNone

DisplayNone is the basic class to handle not displaying anything.

This class has no parameters and will return an empty character.

DisplayNones are created like:

ex_n <- DisplayNone$new()

DisplayTerms

DisplayTerms is the class that holds multiple different DisplayTerm objects. This is the class that you would use to combine multiple types of DisplayTerm objects into one replacement.

DisplayNones are created like:

ex_n <- DisplayTerms$new(contents = list(ex_c, ex_n))

DisplayHeader

DisplayHeader is the class that creates headers and holds DisplayTerm objects.

This class has the following additional parameters:

  • header: The title for the header
  • level: The level of the header
  • link: The link for the header, if there is one

The contents are DisplayTerm objects, meaning that you can combine the generated text with any other DisplayTerm classes.

DisplayHeaders are created like:

ex_h <- DisplayHeader$new(
  header = "Cool Header",
  level = 2,
  contents = ex_n,
  link = "cool_file.md")

There are also several helper functions in this package when it comes to headers.

  • makeHeaderFromList: This is a function that will search a template for a term, find the heading level for it, and create a DisplayHeader
  • listToHeader: This function is wrapped by makeHeaderFromList and turns a list into a DisplayHeader
  • findHeaderLevels: This function is wrapped by makeHeaderFromList and uses regex to find the header level of the term
  • removeHeaderLever: This function can be used to remove the corresponding header levels from a loaded template so that the replacement can work properly
  • makeObsidianFilePath: This will change a file path to just the file name for better usage with Obsidian.

Replacer

The replacer consists of 3 parts:

  • Matcher
  • ReplaceTerm
  • Replacer

Matcher

The Matcher is what character wrap the term in your template.

Keep in mind that regex is used to search for matches in the template. For that reason remember that you need to have regex safe characters and be safe for R escaping as well.

For example, {word} for regex would be \{word\}, but for R you will want to use \\{word\\}.

There are only 2 parameters:

  • left
  • right

Matchers are created like:

matcher <- Matcher$new(left = "\\{", right = "\\}")

ReplaceTerm

The ReplaceTerm is the object that is actually used in the matching. It consists of:

  • contents: A DisplayTerm object
  • search_term: A search term in the template
  • matcher: A Matcher object

ReplaceTerms are created like:

r_days <- ReplaceTerm$new(search_term = "Days",
                          contents = days,
                          matcher = matcher)

Replacer

The Replacer is the object that contains all of the ReplaceTerm objects to use processing your template.

These objects only have one parameter:

  • contents: ReplaceTerm object or list of ReplaceTerm

Replacers are created like:

replacer <- Replacer$new(contents = r_days)

You can also add more terms to an existing Replacer with addTerms.

replacer$addTerms(list(r_weeks, r_months))

A list of the corresponding regex and replacement strings can be extracted with makeReplacement.

replacer$makeReplacement()

Templater

The Templater class is very simple, only having two parameters:

  • replacer: A Replacer object
  • template: A loaded character template.

All you have to do is to do is create and call the Templater like this:

template <- Templater$new(replacer = replacer, 
                          template = template)$process()

By running process you will modify the stored template in place.

The template will only be processed on the intitial process call. On subsequent calls it will just return the stored template. This can be overridden if you pass the force parameter as TRUE.

You can also insert a new template or replacer and they next process call will process the template again.
